opening.headline: After uploading the contract PDF via API to generate a Q&A, where and for how long will that file be retained?
body: To create document-based question-answering, you need to upload files to the provider's storage. Surprisingly few people know whether files remain after the task is complete, or how search indexes are created for retrieval. Files may contain sensitive information such as names, content, and metadata.

In this class, we compare how long Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google's file stores retain files by default, and confirm that original files and vector stores follow different rules. We also examine, through examples, what remains after deletion in the flow from upload to deletion.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the lifecycle and deletion of a file repository.
You can distinguish the retention rules for file repositories and vector repositories.

screens.title: I don't know how long uploaded files will remain.
screens.lead: This is an example case where a Q&A was created using a PDF contract document. Please read it after considering what remains after the work is completed.

visual.alt: File upload, save, and usage flow. Diagram on the right with a question mark indicating deletion status.
labels: When and by whom is deletion performed?

paragraphs: A team uploaded a contract PDF via an API to build a question-answering feature. The demonstration was successfully completed, and the project moved forward to the next phase. However, nobody knows whether the contract PDF is still retained by the provider.

What remains might not be just the original file. It could be indexes created for searching or other derived data. Additionally, retention periods vary by provider: some files disappear after 48 hours, others require explicit expiration settings, and some remain until manually deleted.
The question for this lesson is: who is responsible for removals, and what exactly gets deleted when a deletion request is made?

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Uploading a file requires only one call, but deleting a file often requires separate operations based on location. If you don't design for lifecycle management, the default settings become the policy.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how deletion responsibility is defined in our code.

screens.title: Recall responsibility for deleting uploaded files
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please try answering it yourself before clicking.

items.prompt: Is there also code for deleting files along with the code for uploading files?
items.answer: Upload codes are easily found, but deletion codes are often missing. For each upload point, a deletion timing and the responsible party must be specified. If no deletion code exists, the file remains until its default lifespan expires, or indefinitely.

items.prompt: When you delete a document from the vector repository, do you think the original file is also deleted?
items.answer: They are often separate objects. Even if the original is deleted, an index may remain in the search repository, and conversely, even if the repository is deleted, the original file may still exist. It is necessary to verify, on a per-location basis, which side was deleted.

items.prompt: Do you think a file will automatically disappear if no expiration time is specified?
items.answer: It varies by provider. Some locations automatically delete data 48 hours after it is uploaded, while others retain the data until expiration is specified. Assuming automatic deletion without verifying the default settings can result in data being retained for a longer period.

screens.outro: I will compare in a table how long each of the three providers' file repositories retains files.

screens.title: Comparison of File Repository Lifespans Across Three Providers
screens.lead: The table below compares how Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google's file repositories retain files by default, as well as their policies for expiration and deletion.

data.caption: Basic retention periods and deletion methods for file repositories by provider
rows: Upon upload, you receive `file_id` and retain it until deletion or until reaching `expires_at`. If `expires_at` is not specified, it defaults to `null`.

When uploading, you can set an expiration period between 1 hour and 90 days using `expires_in_seconds`. Once set, the expiration cannot be changed. After expiration, files cannot be downloaded or referenced by request, and metadata can be read for up to 30 days.
Up to 500MB per file, totaling 1TB per organization.
`batch` Files intended for a specific purpose are retained for a default of 30 days; all other files are retained until directly deleted.

`expires_after` with reference time `created_at` and subsecond precision `seconds` allows expiration periods ranging from 1 hour (3,600 seconds) to 30 days (2,592,000 seconds). Manual deletion is also possible.
Up to 512MB per file, 2.5TB per project.
The file is automatically deleted after being stored for 48 hours.
It can also be deleted manually.
20 GB per project, up to 2 GB per file.
data.notes: The default lifespan varies depending on whether automatic deletion, expiration specification, or direct deletion is required. Even for the same file, the retention time can differ significantly based on the provider to which it is uploaded, making it essential to explicitly specify expiration times for each upload. Additionally, since storage limits are independent of lifespan, when uploading large files, always verify both the limit and the retention period.

screens.outro: This includes not only files but also a searchable vector store, so we will distinguish the rules for vector stores in the following screen.

screens.title: The original file and vector repository follow different rules.
screens.lead: Compare how the lifespan differs when the same upload is either the original file or when it's stored in the search repository by alternately selecting between these two states.

states.label: Original file
states.body: This is the original object uploaded via the Files API. In Gemini, the file automatically disappears 48 hours after upload, while in Anthropic and OpenAI, files remain until deletion is explicitly specified. Once a file is deleted in Anthropic, it becomes inaccessible via the API, although it may still remain available for ongoing requests and tool usage. Deleted files cannot be recovered.

states.label: Repository for searches
states.body: OpenAI's file search creates a vector repository and uploads files to serve as a knowledge base. Gemini's file search repository embeddings have no retention period (TTL) and remain stored until the user deletes them; the original Files API objects are deleted 48 hours after creation. In OpenAI's documentation, vector repositories are listed as items that remain until explicitly deleted. Thus, even after the original files are removed, content may still persist in the index. Anthropic and OpenAI classify their file functionality as having persistent state, indicating that it is not subject to the no-retention policy. Therefore, even organizations with no-retention agreements must follow the retention rules of the file functionality when using it. As a result, when the same document is uploaded, the lifespan of the original object and the search-enabled object may differ, requiring individual deletion plans to be established for each object. If this distinction is overlooked, content may continue to appear in search results even after the original files have been deleted.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the lifecycle rules, let's now examine at which point in the flow—from upload to deletion—what remains.

screens.title: Flow from file upload to deletion
screens.lead: When you select the image number marker, you can view the copies generated at each step and those that remain even after deletion.

visual.alt: A horizontal flow diagram illustrating five sequential stages: upload, usage, indexing, deletion, and persistence.
labels: Index, cache, pending requests, our copy

markers.label: upload
markers.title: The file is uploaded to the repository and receives an ID.
markers.body: Once the file is uploaded to the provider's repository, it receives an ID. At this point, its lifespan begins. If an expiration is not specified together, the provider's default value becomes the lifespan.

markers.label: Usage
markers.title: Used in the request with file ID
markers.body: If a file ID is included in the request, the model reads the file. Instead of uploading the file every time, this means that the file remains stored in the repository as long as the ID is active.

markers.label: Indexing
markers.title: Putting it into a search repository creates a copy.
markers.body: When stored in the search repository, the file is split into fragments and an embedded copy is generated. This copy is a separate object from the original and must be managed independently of the original file's deletion.

markers.label: Delete
markers.title: Deleted via delete call or expiration
markers.body: Files are deleted when a delete request is made or when the expiration time is reached. Deleted files cannot be recovered. It is necessary to verify, on a per-location basis, how far the delete request extends.

markers.label: Residual
markers.title: Something that may remain even after deletion
markers.body: The provider's documentation notes that deleted files may remain in ongoing calls and that indexes are treated as separate objects. Together with this, our server's cache and copies should also be independently verified. In particular, our temporary folders, logs, and backups must be manually removed by us, regardless of the provider's deletion actions.

screens.outro: Having followed the flow, I will illustrate with examples how far a deletion request actually extends.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Impact of Deletion Request on Files, Indexes, and Caches
screens.lead: This is a case where a customer requests the deletion of a contract containing personal information. Select the arrow to follow the process in which the instructor verifies the deletion by location.

steps.title: Lists all storage locations
steps.body: First, list all possible locations where a contract document might exist. These include the provider's file storage, vector storage, our server copy, logs, temporary folders, and backups. Locations not listed cannot be deleted.

steps.title: Delete from provider's file repository
steps.body: The file deletion call blocks access to the original. Deleted files cannot be recovered, so verify the file ID again before deletion to ensure the correct target is selected.

steps.title: Deletes documents from the vector repository
steps.body: Documents stored in the vector repository must be deleted separately. If only the original is removed and the index is retained, the content of the contract may continue to appear in search results.

steps.title: We directly delete our copy.
steps.body: Our server copies, logs, temporary folders, and backups are not subject to the provider's deletion request. We are responsible for directly removing them, and the documentation also notes that backups will remain for a specified period based on retention policies. Additionally, the documentation should be considered in relation to the possibility that files deleted during an ongoing request may still remain.

steps.title: Provides evidence of deletion
steps.body: Records, by location and time, when a location was deleted. One line each for provider file, vector repository, server copy, and backup is required to accurately explain the deletion result to the customer.

screens.outro: Having examined the deletion procedure, I will now organize it into design rules.

screens.title: File Lifecycle Design Rules
screens.lead: When you expand each item, you can see the instructor's example of what happens when the rules are not followed.

items.title: Specify expiration when uploading.
items.body: Anthropic can set expiration dates when uploading files to `expires_in_seconds`, and OpenAI can set expiration dates when uploading files to `expires_after`. If no expiration date is specified, files that accidentally omit the deletion code will continue to accumulate. For example, a contract uploaded for demonstration purposes will remain stored in the repository several months later.

items.title: Designate the responsible party for deleting the original, index, and our copy.
items.body: If there is no owner, it's assumed that different teams would have deleted each other's work. By designating an owner for each location, there will be no place where deletion requests go unanswered.

items.title: Files uploaded to the app follow the organization retention settings.
items.body: Files uploaded to apps like claude.ai follow different rules than API file repositories. They are governed by the organization's retention settings and user deletion status. Their lifespan varies depending on the upload path, so they must be managed separately by path.

items.title: File names and metadata are also considered sensitive information.
items.body: There may be cases where file names contain customer names or contract numbers. Even if the content is removed, the name remains and information could leak. There is a method to change file names to values without identifying information before uploading.

items.title: The lifespan is documented based on the value specified in the provider's documentation.
items.body: Basic lifetime and deletion procedures are documented in the team documentation with appropriate context and rationale. This ensures that new team members can share the same assumptions and respond promptly to thanks or customer inquiries.

screens.outro: We have organized the design rules; now I will conclude the previous content in a coherent flow.

screens.title: Consolidation: Files remain if not deleted
screens.lead: Let's go back to the first question and clarify it. Please explain how long and where the uploaded file will remain.

paragraphs: Files uploaded to the file repository remain indefinitely unless deleted. Gemini automatically deletes files after 48 hours, but Anthropic and OpenAI may retain files indefinitely unless an expiration date is specified. Therefore, an expiration date should be set when uploading files.

What remains is not just the original file. The vector repository's index, ongoing requests, our server's copies, logs, and backups each exist separately. Therefore, responsibility for deletion must be assigned by location, and proof of deletion must be retained by location.

Life cycles differ depending on the provider, so it's not appropriate to assume one place's rules directly apply elsewhere. This course concludes with the design of code for uploading and deleting files together.

checks.intro: Recall the lifetime rules of the two repositories you just compared, and answer accordingly. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: Which is appropriate regarding the lifespan of data retrieved from the Gemini File Search repository in relation to the original Files API files?
options: The original content will be deleted after 48 hours, but the storage data will remain until it is intentionally removed.
Repository data is removed first, and the original remains.
Both of them are only retained until the user deletes them, and automatic deletion does not occur.
checks.explain: Even if the original file is deleted, content may remain in the index, so both the original and the repository must be separately deleted.

wrong.0: Data retrieved from the repository is stored indefinitely.
wrong.2: The order is reversed. The original is deleted first.
wrong.3: The original Files API object is automatically deleted after 48 hours.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The original expires after 48 hours, but data retrieved from the storage remains until it is deleted.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The lifespans of two objects are not necessarily the same. Please reconsider which one will be automatically deleted and which one will remain.

checks.intro: Look at the lifecycle of a file in sequence. Scores are not stored.
checks.q: Look at the lifecycle of the file as it resides with the provider, in sequential order.
items: Used in the request with file ID
An index copy is generated when data is stored in the search repository.
Deleted via delete call or expiration
checks.explain: Index, cache, ongoing requests, and our local copies are subject to separate verification even after deletion.
checks.correctFeedback: The lifecycle sequence is accurate. The stages from upload to deletion are well-defined.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Consider again the index copy, based on the fact that it is created when the file is used and then placed into the search repository.

glossary.def: This is the space where the provider stores files uploaded via the API.
A repository that fragments files and indexes them for search purposes.
This action removes an object from the repository. Indices or copies must be verified separately.
This is the period during which data remains, from upload until expiration or deletion.
This field in the Anthropic Files API indicates the timestamp when the file expires.

misconceptions.myth: The file is uploaded and automatically deleted once the operation is complete.
misconceptions.fact: Gemini will be automatically deleted 48 hours after creation, while Anthropic and OpenAI may retain the data until expiration is specified, after which it will be deleted.

misconceptions.myth: Deleting the original file also deletes the search index.
misconceptions.fact: The retrieved data may need to be deleted separately. The original and index must be checked independently.

misconceptions.myth: When the delete API is called, our local copy is also removed.
misconceptions.fact: Server copies, logs, and backups are our responsibility. The provider's delete request applies only to the provider's storage.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The file remains if it is not deleted.
The original file, vector repository, and our copy are each deleted separately.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are intended for you to think about on your own and are not submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where are the files uploaded to our service stored, in what forms, and who removes them?
